title: Cambrian explosion
summary: From about 539 million years ago, almost every major animal body plan appears in the fossil record within some 20 to 30 million years, captured in rare soft-tissue fossil beds in Yunnan, North Greenland and the Canadian Rockies. Why it happened is still debated.
card: The Cambrian explosion is the burst of animal diversification that begins at the base of the Cambrian Period, dated by the International Commission on Stratigraphy to 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago. Over roughly 20 to 30 million years, arthropods, molluscs, brachiopods, worms and the first vertebrates appear, together with active predators, deep burrowers and complex eyes. Exceptionally preserved fossils at Chengjiang, Sirius Passet and the Burgess Shale show these early marine communities in unusual anatomical detail.
what:
The Cambrian explosion is the interval in which the fossil record changes from sparse, mostly soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms and simple trails to diverse animals belonging to most living phyla. The International Commission on Stratigraphy (ICS) places the base of the Cambrian Period, and of the Phanerozoic Eon, at 538.8 ± 0.6 million years ago (Ma) on its current chart (v2026/06); the 2022 and 2023 charts gave the same age with ± 0.2 million years. Zircon dates from Namibia bracket the boundary at 538.6 to 538.8 Ma and indicate that the last Ediacaran-type fossils and the first complex Cambrian burrows are separated by less than about 410,000 years.

Trace fossils record the first stage: the number of burrow types jumps in the Fortunian Age (about 539 to 529 Ma), and in Age 2 (about 529 to 521 Ma) burrowers first mixed seafloor mud thoroughly. On the Siberian Platform, skeletal stem-group molluscs and brachiopods diversify through the Terreneuvian, while their crown groups radiate from about 522 Ma. Three Lagerstätten, deposits that preserve soft tissue, show the animals themselves. The Chengjiang biota of Yunnan, China, has a maximum age of 518.03 ± 0.71 Ma and records at least 16 phyla and about 196 species, vertebrates among them; UNESCO's 2012 inscription uses an older figure of 530 Ma. The Sirius Passet biota of Peary Land, North Greenland, about 519 Ma (Cambrian Stage 3), is dominated by predators and swimmers that lived in water very low in oxygen. The Burgess Shale on Fossil Ridge in Yoho National Park, British Columbia, found by Charles Walcott in 1909, is younger, about 505 Ma, and records the middle Cambrian tail of the radiation.

Specialists disagree on its tempo and causes: some see two phases separated by the Sinsk extinction around 513 Ma, others a protracted process of more than 22 million years or one of several radiations reaching back to about 571 Ma, while molecular clocks place animal origins well before the first fossils. Proposed causes, often combined, are rising oxygen, escalating predator–prey ecology and new developmental gene networks.

uncertainty.note: Start is the ICS base of the Cambrian, 538.8 ± 0.6 Ma; Zhuravlev & Wood (2018) place the onset of skeletal diversification at about 542 Ma, and Wood et al. (2019) see earlier radiations from about 571 Ma. End is the Sinsk extinction, about 513 Ma (Zhuravlev & Wood 2018); Wood et al. (2019) bound the explosion at about 520 Ma, while the Burgess Shale (about 505 Ma) and the continuation into the Ordovician radiation extend the tail later.

how: Sequence and mechanism as currently reconstructed: (1) By the late Ediacaran, from about 571 Ma, soft-bodied macro-organisms and simple bilaterian trails already existed on seafloors bound by microbial mats, and drill holes in the tube fossil Cloudina show predation before the Cambrian began. (2) Across the boundary at 538.8 Ma the Ediacaran biota disappears within a window of about 410,000 years and complex probing burrows such as Treptichnus pedum spread; in the Fortunian the diversity of burrow forms rises faster than at any other time. (3) In Age 2 deep burrowing and sediment mixing replace mat-bound seafloors (the agronomic revolution), pushing oxygen and food into the sediment and opening new niches. (4) Mineralised skeletons, jointed limbs, eyes and active predation spread, and food webs gain tiers; Chengjiang and Sirius Passet show predator-rich communities by about 519 to 518 Ma, some living in water with only 0.2 to 0.4 ml of oxygen per litre. (5) The Sinsk event around 513 Ma removes many stem groups, including archaeocyath reefs, while crown-group lineages continue into the Ordovician. Soft tissues survive at the Lagerstätten because animals were buried in fine, low-oxygen mud below storm wave base, at the Burgess Shale probably by underwater mudflows. Proposed drivers are rising oxygen that made energetically costly carnivory possible, escalating predator–prey and engineering feedbacks, developmental gene regulatory networks assembled tens of millions of years earlier, and pulses of redox and nutrient change; most authors combine several.
why_it_matters: The Cambrian explosion set out the basic anatomical designs of most animal phyla living today, including the chordate line that leads to fish and, much later, to humans; the early vertebrates of Chengjiang are among its oldest known members. It also assembled the first ecosystems that look modern: predators and prey, burrowers that mixed and ventilated the seafloor, and food webs several tiers deep, which changed how carbon and nutrients cycle through the oceans. Its starting point is the base of the Phanerozoic Eon, so the geological time scale used by every later record on this globe is anchored to it, and later crises and recoveries, from the Sinsk event to the Ordovician radiation and the end-Permian extinction, are measured against the body plans established here. The Lagerstätten matter in their own right: without the rare soft-tissue windows of Chengjiang, Sirius Passet and the Burgess Shale, the radiation would be known almost only from shells and burrows, and the long argument over whether animals arose suddenly or had hidden earlier histories would lack its central evidence. If the molecular-clock view of deep roots is correct, the event records less the birth of animals than the moment they became large, mobile, armoured and fossilisable. Today the Burgess Shale and Chengjiang are protected World Heritage properties whose fossils remain a principal test of how environment and ecology steer evolution.

related.title: Ediacaran biota
related.because: Late Ediacaran organisms supplied ancestral animal lineages and the microbial-mat seafloors that Cambrian burrowers and predators then transformed.

related.title: Neoproterozoic oxygenation event
related.because: Rising ocean oxygen is argued to have allowed energetically costly carnivory and larger, more active animals, although its timing and magnitude remain disputed.

related.title: Great Ordovician Biodiversification Event
related.because: Crown-group lineages that radiated in the Cambrian and survived the Sinsk event supplied the stock that diversified further in the Ordovician radiation.

perspectives.holder: Oxygenation as environmental trigger (e.g. Sperling et al. 2013; Wood et al. 2019)
perspectives.account: Rising and fluctuating ocean oxygen and nutrient supply are argued to have enabled the radiation: in modern low-oxygen zones carnivores are scarce, so oxygen thresholds may have gated predation and complex food webs, explaining the timing; Wood and colleagues tie successive radiations to dynamic redox changes.

perspectives.holder: Tolerance of low oxygen challenges a simple oxygen trigger (e.g. Hammarlund et al. 2019; Mángano & Buatois 2020)
perspectives.account: Geochemistry at Sirius Passet indicates a diverse predator community living at roughly 0.2 to 0.4 ml of oxygen per litre, and trace-fossil workers argue early animals tolerated dysoxia and may have helped raise oxygen themselves, so oxygen is seen as permissive rather than the fundamental trigger.

perspectives.holder: Ecological escalation and ecosystem engineering (e.g. Linnemann et al. 2019; Mángano & Buatois 2020; Harper et al. 2019)
perspectives.account: Predator–prey arms races and the spread of mobile burrowers drove ecological cascades: the Ediacaran-to-Cambrian faunal turnover within about 410,000 years, the replacement of mat seafloors by mixed sediment, and predator-dominated communities point to feedbacks among animals themselves as the engine of diversification.

perspectives.holder: Developmental genetics and deep roots (e.g. Erwin et al. 2011; dos Reis et al. 2015)
perspectives.account: Molecular clocks and comparative developmental data suggest animal lineages and their gene regulatory toolkits arose in the Cryogenian or Ediacaran, tens of millions of years before their first fossils; the explosion is then an ecological and preservational release of pre-existing lineages, though clock precision is too low to match dates to specific environmental events.

perspectives.holder: Tempo: one burst versus a protracted or multi-phase radiation (e.g. Zhuravlev & Wood 2018; Yang et al. 2018; Wood et al. 2019)
perspectives.account: Rather than a single short event, the radiation is described as two phases separated by the Sinsk extinction near 513 Ma, as a process lasting more than 22 million years up to Chengjiang time, or as one of several transitional radiations from the late Ediacaran into the early Palaeozoic.

importance.justification: The appearance of nearly all animal phyla marks the base of the Phanerozoic and underlies every later chapter of animal life, so it must be visible at whole-planet zoom.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the paleo-positions (PALEOMAP and MERDITH2021 differ by ~56° latitude for South China, and MERDITH2021 gave no result for the Burgess Shale) and of the end date, which depends on how authors bound the radiation; several peer-reviewed sources were read at abstract level only, and the Burgess Shale point is a ridge midpoint, not a surveyed quarry coordinate.
